analysis.one_liner: Raises fines on hospitals that refuse to publish their standard prices for care.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal rules already require hospitals to publish a list of their standard charges, but the current fine tops out at about $300 per day, which is trivial for large hospitals. This bill raises the fine dramatically for big hospitals — up to $11,000 per day — makes the fine rules permanent, bars hospitals from hiding their price pages from online search engines, and requires the government to publish a public list of hospitals that are out of compliance.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and anyone shopping for care: hospitals would have to publish real, machine-readable price lists they couldn't hide from search results, making it possible to compare what care costs before getting a bill.

how_it_helps.text: Increases the daily civil monetary penalty for hospitals that fail to publish and update their standard charge lists, with larger hospitals facing fines up to $11,000 per day instead of the small fine currently in law [S2][S3].
Prohibits hospitals from using webpage coding to shield their required price information from online search results, so published prices are actually findable [S3].
Requires the Secretary of Health and Human Services to publish a public list of every hospital out of compliance, updated every 180 days [S3].
Sets firm timing requirements: existing hospitals must post prices within six months of enactment and update them yearly [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals — mostly large ones — that do not comply with the transparency rules would face much steeper fines and public name-and-shame listings. The compliance itself (publishing price lists) is a modest administrative cost.

drawbacks.text: Fines and publication requirements do not by themselves make hospital prices fair or low; a hospital can comply fully with a list of chargemaster prices that no insurer pays and no patient can navigate, so transparency may not translate into savings for many patients.

The penalty structure still lets small hospitals off lightly ($600 per day for hospitals with 30 or fewer beds), and enforcement depends entirely on the Health and Human Services Secretary actually imposing penalties [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a genuine but narrow fix: it gives real teeth to a transparency rule whose current fines are too small to matter to large hospital systems. It does not cap prices or lower bills directly — it only makes prices visible — so its benefit depends on patients, employers, and insurers actually using the published data to push costs down. The administrative cost to hospitals is small; the risk is that transparency alone underdelivers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate health committee, where it sat until the Congress ended — no hearing, no vote, no cosponsors.

narrative.text: Sen. John Kennedy introduced the bill on February 16, 2023 [S1][S5].
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which was its last action in the 118th Congress [S5].
No senator signed on as a cosponsor [S4], and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals that fail to publish their standard prices are better off, because the fine increase and the public non-compliance list never became law. Patients are left with the same weak enforcement.

for.name: Sen. John Kennedy
for.role: U.S. Senator from Louisiana and bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Hospital Transparency Compliance Enforcement Act and referred it to committee

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction, chaired by Sen. Bernie Sanders (D)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it died in committee after two years

sides.party_line_note: The bill got no cosponsors from either party and never reached a vote, so no party-line split was ever recorded; the sponsor was a Republican.

industries.note: The bill raises daily fines up to $11,000 for large hospitals that fail to publish standard charges, bans hiding price pages from search engines, and requires a public list of non-compliant hospitals. Hospitals benefit financially from price opacity, so their interest runs against patients here.
Negotiating better hospital rates is easier when standard charge lists are complete, current, and findable; employers and insurers shopping for care are among the main intended users of the data.
